worksheets.title: QBI Deduction Worksheet
worksheets.description: Organize business income, wage/property limits, SSTB risk, and phaseout assumptions before you estimate or defend a QBI deduction.
opening: Most QBI mistakes happen because people skip the worksheet and jump straight to the answer they want.
This worksheet forces the ugly parts into the open: what counts as qualified income, where the phaseout risk shows up, and what support your CPA will need.
howTo: Use this before you start arguing about the deduction amount. The job is to get the facts, thresholds, and weak assumptions in one place.
If the worksheet exposes SSTB risk, wage-limit friction, or messy entity splits, treat that as the point of the exercise, not a reason to keep guessing.

faq.q: Why use a worksheet if my software already estimates QBI?
faq.a: Because software can still produce a number from bad assumptions. The worksheet makes the controlling facts visible before you trust the output.

faq.q: What usually breaks a QBI estimate?
faq.a: SSTB ambiguity, owner-level taxable income changes, and wage or property limits that were never documented clearly.

faq.q: When should I fill this out?
faq.a: At midyear for planning and again before filing, especially if income moved or the entity structure changed.

worksheets.title: S-Corp Election Decision Worksheet
worksheets.description: Write down tax savings, payroll reality, admin burden, and reasonable-salary assumptions before you elect S-corp treatment.
opening: S-corp election conversations usually start with tax savings and end with admin pain. That is backward.
This worksheet is for deciding whether the election still makes sense after you account for payroll, reasonable salary, compliance work, and cash-flow reality.
howTo: Use this before filing the election. The worksheet is supposed to surface the friction early, not after payroll is already live.
If the savings only work when the salary assumption is aggressive or the admin burden is ignored, write that down plainly.

fieldGroups.title: Current Business Snapshot
fieldGroups.hint: Start with what the business actually looks like now.

fields.label: Current entity / filing setup
fields.placeholder: Single-member LLC, partnership, sole prop, etc.

fields.label: Expected annual net income
fields.placeholder: Planning number

fields.label: What work does the owner actually perform?
fields.placeholder: Sales, operations, delivery, management, etc.

fieldGroups.title: Tax and Payroll Assumptions
fieldGroups.hint: These assumptions decide whether the election is durable or fake.

fields.label: Reasonable salary assumption
fields.placeholder: What number are you using and why?

fields.label: Projected payroll/self-employment tax savings
fields.placeholder: Estimate

fields.label: Payroll, filings, and bookkeeping readiness
fields.placeholder: Who will run payroll, handle deposits, file forms, and keep the books clean?

fieldGroups.title: Decision Pressure Test
fieldGroups.hint: Write the parts that would make you hesitate.

fields.label: Admin burden or compliance friction
fields.placeholder: What extra work or cost comes with the election?

fields.label: Cash-flow risk or payroll risk
fields.placeholder: What happens in a weak month?

fields.label: Questions for CPA or payroll advisor
fields.placeholder: List the issues that need a real answer before filing

checklist: Do not rely on tax savings without writing down the salary assumption that creates them.
Write down who owns payroll and compliance before the election is filed.
Keep the worksheet with any reasonable-salary support and payroll setup notes.

faq.q: What is the point of this worksheet if I already have an S-corp calculator?
faq.a: The calculator estimates savings. The worksheet tells you whether the election still makes sense after payroll, compliance, and cash-flow reality.

faq.q: What makes this decision go bad most often?
faq.a: Aggressive salary assumptions, sloppy payroll execution, and treating the election like a tax trick instead of an operating change.
Before you file the election and again before payroll goes live if income or role assumptions changed.

worksheets.title: Tax-Loss Harvesting Worksheet
worksheets.description: Track positions, replacement trades, wash-sale risk, and gain-offset goals before you start harvesting losses in a taxable portfolio.
opening: Tax-loss harvesting sounds simple until the wash-sale rule and the replacement trade start fighting each other.
This worksheet helps you write down the trade, the replacement, the expected tax use, and the parts of the plan most likely to blow up in execution.
howTo: Use this before you place the trade, not after. The point is to decide what you are replacing and what tax effect you are actually targeting.
If the worksheet shows a wash-sale problem, unclear holding periods, or no real gain-offset use, stop and clean that up first.

fieldGroups.title: Position and Goal
fieldGroups.hint: Start with the trade you are considering and why.

fields.label: Position or fund you may sell
fields.placeholder: Ticker or holding name

fields.label: Estimated unrealized loss
fields.placeholder: Rough amount

fields.label: Tax goal for this harvest
fields.placeholder: Offset gains, build carryforward, rebalance, reduce concentration, etc.

fieldGroups.title: Replacement and Wash-Sale Review
fieldGroups.hint: Write down the part most people skip.

fields.label: Replacement security or strategy
fields.placeholder: What will you own instead?

fields.label: Wash-sale risk note
fields.placeholder: Any automatic buys, spouse accounts, DRIPs, or recent purchases?

fields.label: Holding-period or timing note
fields.placeholder: Anything about the trade timing that matters?

fieldGroups.title: Expected Tax Use and Review
fieldGroups.hint: Write down what the harvested loss is actually for.

fields.label: What gain or income will this loss offset?
fields.placeholder: Expected gains this year, carryforward use, etc.

fields.label: Documentation gaps or trade-confirm issues
fields.placeholder: What would make this hard to support later?

fields.label: Questions for advisor or tax planner
fields.placeholder: List the things that need review before the trade executes

checklist: Write down the replacement trade before you sell the loss position.
Check for wash-sale risk across automatic buys, spouse accounts, and related accounts.
Keep confirms, lot data, and the worksheet in the same folder.

faq.q: Why use a worksheet if my brokerage already shows unrealized losses?
faq.a: Because the brokerage does not explain the replacement trade, the wash-sale exposure, or what tax purpose the harvest is actually serving.
People chase the loss, forget the replacement, and create a wash-sale or a portfolio move they did not really want.

faq.q: When should I use this worksheet?
faq.a: Before harvesting any loss that matters. If the trade is meaningful enough to celebrate, it is meaningful enough to document.
